scenes.tts: A gradient can bring an axon to the right neighbourhood. But a thin layer is either the right one, or it is not. In the retina, each cell type sends its processes into one or a few sublaminae. How does a process choose? Discrete choices often call for discrete labels.
scenes.visual: A gradient brings an axon to a glowing target; the target resolves into thin layers; processes hover with question marks over which layer; then labels are named.
scenes.narration: A gradient can bring an axon to the right neighbourhood. But a thin layer is either the right one, or it is not. In the retina, each cell type sends its processes into one or a few sublaminae. How does a process choose? Discrete choices often call for discrete labels.

scenes.tts: In chick retina, two proteins, Sidekick one and Sidekick two, are made by largely separate groups of neurons. The processes of each group end in different sublaminae. Each protein binds its own kind, which is called homophilic binding. Cells carrying Sidekick one stick to other cells carrying Sidekick one.
scenes.visual: Two layers carry yellow and blue labels; yellow and blue cells send processes that end in their matching layer; matching knobs lock.
scenes.caption: In chick retina, two proteins, Sidekick-1 and Sidekick-2, are made by largely separate groups of neurons. The processes of each group end in different sublaminae. Each protein binds its own kind, which is called homophilic binding. Cells carrying Sidekick-1 stick to other cells carrying Sidekick-1.
scenes.narration: In chick retina, two proteins, Sidekick-1 and Sidekick-2, are made by largely separate groups of neurons. The processes of each group end in different sublaminae. Each protein binds its own kind, which is called homophilic binding. Cells carrying Sidekick-1 stick to other cells carrying Sidekick-1.

scenes.tts: The key test was misexpression, which means making a protein in a cell that normally lacks it. Retinal neurons were made to produce a Sidekick they did not normally make. Their processes shifted toward the sublamina where that Sidekick was already concentrated. So a label biases where an arbor ends. It is one part of how layers form, not the whole.
scenes.visual: A grey cell gets the yellow label and its arbor moves up to the yellow layer.

scenes.tts: Now the opposite problem. A neuron must keep its own branches apart, which is called self-avoidance. In the fly, the protein Dscam one also binds mainly to identical forms. But here the outcome is repulsion, so two touching branches with the same forms pull apart. Without Dscam one, fly sensory neurons have dendrites that cross and bundle with their own branches.
scenes.visual: Two branches of one purple neuron meet, matching tips lock then pull apart; then the case without Dscam1 where they cross and bundle.

scenes.tts: To tell itself from its neighbours, a fly sensory neuron needs its own surface identity. A single fly gene, Dscam one, can be spliced into thirty-eight thousand and sixteen forms. Each neuron appears to express a small, partly random subset, and a large menu keeps accidental matches rare. Its own branches match, so they pull apart, while branches of other neurons do not match and can overlap.
scenes.visual: Two neurons overlap; a menu of forms appears; each neuron picks a small different subset; own branches pull apart, neighbours overlap.

scenes.tts: Gradients give continuous order, while labels give discrete membership, such as a layer, or self versus other. The same chemistry can serve opposite ends. Matching Sidekick draws processes together. Matching Dscam one drives branches apart. What the cell does after the bond forms decides which.
scenes.visual: A smooth ramp versus steps; then one matching bond with two outcomes, together and apart.
